opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think the honest answer is: a lot more than people intuitively assume, but the bottleneck isn't really money. It's the form of the data.

If you're talking about teleoperation data, where someone is directly controlling a robot to collect demonstrations, even a very well-funded company is constrained. You need physical robots, operators, maintenance, resets, and every hour of data costs real hardware time. The largest efforts today are in the range of tens of thousands to maybe a few hundred thousand hours. That sounds big, but compared to the internet-scale text or video that language and vision models train on, it's tiny. Teleoperation scales roughly linearly with the number of robots and people, so you can't spend your way to orders-of-magnitude growth easily.

Where it gets interesting is if you move away from requiring a robot in the loop. That's a direction my lab has been very excited about: collecting human data directly. People wear egocentric cameras, maybe lightweight sensors like gloves or wrist-mounted devices, and just go about doing tasks, cooking, cleaning, assembling things. There's no robot involved, so the cost per hour drops dramatically and you can parallelize across thousands or even millions of people.

A wealthy company that seriously invested in this, say by deploying wearable capture devices across a large workforce or partnering with people who already do manual work all day, could plausibly reach millions of hours of high-quality human manipulation data within a year or two. That starts to approach the scale where you see emergent generalization in other domains.

The catch, and this is the research problem, is that human data isn't robot data. Human hands aren't robot grippers, human bodies move differently, and the viewpoint and dynamics don't match. So the real question isn't just how much you can collect, but how efficiently you can transfer it, how you bridge the embodiment gap so that a million hours of humans doing things actually becomes useful robot capability. I think whoever solves that transfer problem well will find data is no longer the limiting factor it is today.

r001.rationale: The response estimates millions of hours of human-captured manipulation data from wearable collection, but does not estimate roughly one to two million hours from buying everyone’s available robot-learning data.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and the honest answer is: it depends entirely on what you count as "human data."

If you mean data that's actually in the right format for robot learning, meaning teleoperation data where a person is directly driving a robot through a task, the number is surprisingly small, even for a company with effectively unlimited money. The bottleneck isn't dollars, it's throughput. A teleoperator produces maybe a few hours of usable demonstrations per day, and you need the hardware, the operators, the task setups, and a pipeline to make sure the data isn't garbage. If you ran something like a thousand robots with a thousand operators, around the clock for a year, you're looking at on the order of a few million hours. That sounds like a lot until you compare it to language models, which train on the equivalent of millions of lifetimes of human writing. So we're talking about something like a few orders of magnitude less than what made LLMs work, and that's the optimistic scenario.

Now, if you widen the definition to include human video, things like first-person footage of people doing everyday tasks, then the picture changes. YouTube alone has billions of hours of people manipulating objects. A well-funded company could also go out and collect egocentric video at a massive scale with head-mounted cameras, and that's cheap compared to teleop. The catch is that this data doesn't come with actions. You can see what the hand did, but the robot has to figure out how to map that onto its own body, and that embodiment gap is still one of the hard open problems. So you can assemble a lot of it, but whether it's actually "robot learning data" depends on whether your learning method can use it.

The middle ground that I find most interesting is these hand-held or wearable data collection devices, where a person uses something that's shaped like the robot's gripper but isn't attached to a robot. You get real action labels and real contact, and you can hand these out to hundreds of people and have them walk around collecting data in homes and kitchens. That could realistically give you tens of millions of trajectories in a year if you were serious about it.

So my rough breakdown would be: teleop, on the order of millions of hours if you throw everything at it. Wearable or proxy-device data, maybe an order of magnitude more. Human video, essentially unlimited, but with the caveat that it's the hardest to actually learn from. And I think the real question for the field isn't how much can you collect, it's which of those tiers your algorithm can actually convert into capability. Right now, the money is way ahead of the methods.

r001.rationale: The response estimates “a few million hours” from a hypothetical thousand-robot teleoperation effort, but does not say that a company could assemble roughly one to two million hours by buying everyone’s available robot-learning data.

astra-6.text:
It depends on what you mean by human data. If you mean videos of people doing things, a very wealthy company could collect a huge amount. But if you mean demonstrations that a robot can directly learn from—with the actions, observations, and outcomes recorded together—that’s a much harder collection problem.

You could put a lot of money into people operating robots and build a large dataset today. The question is whether that data covers enough variation: different objects, different environments, and what happens when something goes wrong. A million repetitions of the same task aren’t necessarily as useful as a smaller dataset that captures those differences.

So I don’t have a precise number, but I think money can buy substantial scale. What it doesn’t automatically buy is the right data, or a system that can turn all of it into broadly useful robot behavior.

r001.rationale: The response gives no estimate of roughly one to two million hours and does not say a company could buy everyone’s available robot-learning data.

sol-6.1.text:
If you mean video of people doing things, a wealthy company could collect a huge amount. But if you mean data that directly teaches a robot how to act, that’s a much harder question. Watching someone pick up a cup doesn’t tell you the forces they applied, what they felt, or how they corrected when it started to slip.

So I’d separate the amount of human activity you can record from the amount of useful robot training data you can get out of it. You could invest in collecting demonstrations at scale, but you’d still need a way to translate those demonstrations into actions for a particular robot. My guess is that the bottleneck would quickly become that translation and the quality and diversity of the data, rather than simply how many hours you can afford to record.

r001.rationale: The response does not estimate roughly one to two million hours of high-quality data; it only describes the amount as “huge” and discusses data limitations.
